Trader Joe’s settles class action lawsuit — you may be in for a big payout Updated: 5:22 PM EDT Apr 16, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ If you’ve been a loyal Trader Joe’s shopper for the past few years, that loyalty may actually pay off. The popular grocery chain has agreed to settle a class action lawsuit filed against the company back in 2019, which alleged that Trader Joe’s violated the Fair and Accurate Credit Transactions Act (FACTA) at some of its stores. The lawsuit claimed that certain Trader Joe’s locations printed receipts showing both the first six and last four digits of customers’ credit or debit card numbers, a practice that can increase the risk of identity theft. Under FACTA, businesses are prohibited from printing more than the last five digits of a customer’s card number on receipts.Trader Joe’s has maintained that not all of its stores printed receipts this way and that, even among the stores that did, only a small number of transactions were affected. Still, the company has agreed to settle the case for $7.4 million.The chain has also denied any wrongdoing and says there have been no known cases of identity theft tied to the receipts in question. According to the settlement terms, Trader Joe’s agreed to resolve the case in order to avoid further litigation.The settlement still needs final court approval and is scheduled for a hearing in August 2026. If it is approved, some customers may qualify for a payout.Eligible customers include those who made a purchase at Trader Joe’s between March 5, 2019, and July 19, 2019, used a credit or debit card, and received a receipt showing the first six and last four digits of their card number. Anyone who is unsure whether they qualify can visit the settlement website for more information and to submit a claim.If the settlement receives final approval, eligible customers will receive $102.45, and checks will be mailed within 10 business days of that approval. It happened Monday morning in the San Fernando Valley community of Pacoima, California. Video shows a low-flying plane strike a power line, triggering a small explosion, before plummeting about 30 feet to a parking lot below. According to officials with the Los Angeles Fire Department, a 70-year-old man was flying the Cessna 172.After striking the power line, the plane nosedived into an O'Reilly’s auto shop parking lot below.Local news outlets report that the plane was returning to the nearby Whiteman Airport at the time of the crash. The pilot, who was the only person in the plane, was taken to a nearby hospital for treatment. His condition is unknown.No additional injuries were reported.Officials with the Federal Aviation Administration say the crash is under investigation. Weather Information Top Picks Local sustainable toy company is collecting and repairing used stuffed animals to reduce waste The owner of The Bunny Bin says cleaning and re-selling old toys keeps them out of landfills Next Story Local sustainable toy company is collecting and repairing used stuffed animals to reduce waste The owner of The Bunny Bin says cleaning and re-selling old toys keeps them out of landfills Updated: 7:04 PM EDT Apr 22, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ A local business is repairing old stuffed animals and finding them new homes. The Bunny Bin, a new sustainable toy company, is rescuing and reselling used stuffed animals in an effort to keep toys in homes and out of landfills. Kate Niemczyk, founder of The Bunny Bin, said she has always cared about the environment. "It's always been part of my life just growing up here in Vermont. I participated in Green Up Day as a kid," said Niemczyk. Now, she's combining her passion for sustainability with her love of toys. "I'm a huge animal lover and that started as being a huge stuffed animal lover," Niemczyk said. This past December she launched a sustainable toy company, to keep toys in circulation longer. Niemczyk said she started the company after noticing that fewer people were buying stuffed animals second-hand compared to other toy types. "I think there's concern around stuffies being cleaned. And so that's why I have a process to clean them after rescuing them," she said. To counter these concerns, Niemczyk came up with a cleaning process to encourage people to refurbish their animals, rather than throwing them away. Through The Bunny Bin, she hopes to reduce plastic toy waste. She also hopes to erase the stigma around buying used products. Niemczyk said she's received a large number of donations so far. One third grade class in Burlington even scheduled a donation drop-off, with every student bringing in an animal. "It was like this beautiful day of meeting these kids who were so generous. They had written bios about, you know, their toy," she said. Niemczyk said you can coordinate a stuffed animal donation pickup or buy a toy online.
